name: SLAP lesion (superior labral anterior-posterior tear)
aliases: superior labrum anterior to posterior tear

reference.source: Miller's Review of Orthopaedics / Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
clinicalPearls: A tear of the superior glenoid labrum centred on the biceps anchor, extending anterior and posterior to the attachment of the long head of biceps tendon
Typical mechanisms are a fall onto an outstretched hand, a traction injury, or repetitive overhead throwing (the peel-back mechanism in athletes)
Patients describe deep shoulder pain, painful clicking or catching, and loss of throwing velocity rather than frank instability
Provocative tests such as O'Brien active compression, the crank test and the biceps load tests support the diagnosis but none is highly specific
Commonly classified into types I-IV (Snyder), with type II (detachment of the labrum and biceps anchor) the most frequently treated surgically
MR arthrography is more sensitive than plain MRI, but asymptomatic labral change is common with age so imaging must be correlated clinically
Coexisting rotator cuff pathology, internal impingement and instability are frequent and influence management
reference.pathophysiology: The superior labrum anchors the long head of biceps tendon to the supraglenoid tubercle. Acute traction or compression loads, or the repetitive torsional and peel-back forces of overhead throwing, avulse or fray the superior labrum and destabilise the biceps-labral complex. This disrupts the labral contribution to glenohumeral concavity-compression and biceps load transfer, producing pain and mechanical symptoms; in throwers it often coexists with posterosuperior internal impingement and a glenohumeral internal rotation deficit.
additionalDifferentials: Long head of biceps tendinopathy or subluxation
Cervical radiculopathy referring to the shoulder
additionalInvestigations: Plain radiographs to exclude bony and other joint pathology
Magnetic resonance arthrography of the shoulder
Standard MRI where arthrography is unavailable
Diagnostic arthroscopy as the definitive assessment
Assessment for glenohumeral internal rotation deficit in throwers
redFlags: Recurrent frank dislocation suggesting significant instability rather than an isolated labral tear
Rapidly progressive weakness or a mass suggesting biceps rupture or tumour
Night pain and constitutional symptoms prompting exclusion of neoplasia or infection
reference.prognosis: Many SLAP lesions, particularly in older patients or as incidental findings, respond to rehabilitation; surgically treated type II tears in young athletes have variable return-to-sport rates, and outcomes of repair versus biceps tenodesis depend on age, activity and associated pathology.
pitfalls: Over-diagnosing symptomatic SLAP tears from MRI when age-related labral change is incidental
Attempting labral repair in older patients in whom biceps tenodesis or non-operative care gives better results
Missing associated rotator cuff or instability lesions that drive symptoms
Relying on any single provocative test given their limited specificity
references: Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
management: Offer first-line structured physiotherapy targeting rotator cuff and scapular strengthening, posterior capsular stretching and correction of glenohumeral internal rotation deficit in throwers
Provide analgesia and activity or throwing modification, with a corticosteroid injection for symptom control
Undertake arthroscopic labral repair for symptomatic unstable type II tears in young athletes who fail rehabilitation
Prefer biceps tenodesis or tenotomy in older patients or where degenerative change accompanies the tear
Address concomitant pathology such as rotator cuff tears or a paralabral cyst at the same procedure
Guide graduated return-to-sport rehabilitation with realistic counselling on the variable recovery of throwing performance
